tagline: A refuge drive through the lakes of a glacial valley.
intro: The Des Lacs refuge drive takes in Upper, Middle and Lower Des Lacs lakes and the town of Kenmare. Interpretive panels stand along the route. The refuge extends from the Canadian border to near Kenmare, along Des Lacs Lake.

Meltwater from two large glacial lakes cut steep valleys here around 10,000 years ago. Early trappers used the name Riviere des Lacs, meaning River of the Lakes. The refuge was established in 1935 to protect waterfowl. Its creation was a Civilian Conservation Corps project.

Kenmare and the Lower, Middle and Upper Des Lacs lakes are anchors of the refuge drive. The refuge’s nature trails include Munch’s Coulee, Canada Goose, White-tailed Deer and the informal trails at Tasker’s Coulee.

moments.title: Munch's Coulee Trail
moments.text: Munch’s Coulee is one of the nature trails at Des Lacs National Wildlife Refuge. The refuge protects waterfowl habitat, with tens of thousands of birds using it for migration and breeding.

moments.title: Kenmare
moments.text: Grain once reached Kenmare by barge on the Des Lacs River before continuing on the Soo Line. Railway extensions had increased access to the region: the Great Northern arrived in 1886 and the Soo Line in 1893. Valley settlement accelerated after 1896, and Kenmare was platted in 1897. The river’s grain traffic was brief. The refuge drive now passes through the town as part of its route among the three Des Lacs lakes.

moments.title: Des Lacs National Wildlife Refuge
moments.text: The 19,500-acre refuge protects a valley shaped by glacial meltwater. Water spilling from two glacial lakes cut the steep valley sides. Waterfowl protection has involved construction as well as setting land aside. In the 1990s, eight artificial islands were built as nesting habitat, primarily for mallards, gadwalls and Canada geese. The islands were not maintained because of cost and ceased to provide effective protection from predators.
